title: Fire and smoke restoration
estimatedMinutesNote: Estimated, not verified. Rule: learner text 3392 words / 100 per minute + 3 min per knowledge check (12) + 5 min allowance, rounded to nearest 5, minimum 15.

instruction.heading: Module authority and restricted work
instruction.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a fire-damaged building, to release or re-occupy it, to disturb structures, utilities, asbestos-suspect material or hazardous residue, to handle or dispose of waste, or to certify that a property is safe, clean or free of contamination. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Fire-scene release, structural and utility isolation, asbestos assessment and removal, and some waste handling are restricted to competent and, where the law requires, licensed people, and may be controlled by fire investigators, the police, structural engineers, utilities or the building owner. Insurer and owner permission do not replace a release from the authority that controls the site. Where that authority is not identified, do not proceed.

instruction.heading: 1. Authorisation and fire-scene release
instruction.body: Authority and access are assessed only after access, permitted tasks and responsibility are established. An owner may ask for immediate salvage while the fire investigation or structural survey has not released the premises. Ask who controls access, what has been formally released and which safety reviews are still open. Customer urgency is never a substitute for verification. Check the written authority that controls the property, the scope of permitted access and any restriction on disturbing contents. Where clearance is ambiguous, remain outside and request confirmation from the responsible authority. Before acting, record the site evidence, the decision owner, the uncertainties and any specialists needed. An unverified scene-release claim must stop work. In training, compare three mock release documents and decide which, if any, permits the proposed activity. Record why keys or a verbal permission on their own are insufficient. The handover from this stage should state the scope, the observations, the unresolved hazards, the consent or authority held, the responsible professional and the next review step.

instruction.heading: 2. Post-fire structural and utility hazards
instruction.body: A room may look stable while a damaged electrical distribution board or a sagging ceiling is visible in photographs. Use non-intrusive visual observation only. Treat damaged wiring, gas lines, overhead loads, weakened stairs and unstable walls as stop-work hazards. Qualified utility and structural personnel decide on isolation and entry permissions, and no entry is made until competent parties have resolved these hazards. In training, mark unsafe entry routes on a mock floor plan and produce a referral request. Do not propose do-it-yourself electrical or structural work.

instruction.heading: 3. Ash, soot and combustion-residue exposure
instruction.body: Ash and combustion residues are uncertain material. Assume that their composition is not known, keep the dust undisturbed, assess the respiratory and surface hazards, and identify the qualified cleaning methods approved for the site. Visible soil removal is not the same as exposure control, so a clean-looking surface is not evidence that the residue is gone. Do not dry-disturb unidentified residues. A proposal to sweep black powder from a burned office with a domestic vacuum must be refused, because it would disturb the material and spread fine particles. In training, use sample material photographs and a task-risk worksheet to select the escalation, the zoning and the equipment-review steps.

instruction.heading: 4. Asbestos and legacy hazardous materials
instruction.body: Before touching any material, determine the age of the building and check any prior records of hazardous materials. Fire-damaged asbestos-containing material may become friable, so ceiling sheeting and insulation of unknown composition must not be disturbed. Qualified investigation and, where the local rules require it, licensed removal may be needed. Requirements differ between states and territories. In training, prepare an asbestos-suspect stop-work notification based on a fictional site record, and identify the competent assessment that is missing.

instruction.heading: 5. Site zoning and occupant protection
instruction.body: Define the exclusion areas and make the access decisions with the site controller. Consider vulnerable occupants, adjacent occupied areas and the movement of contaminated materials. A neighbouring tenant may want to walk through a partly damaged corridor to collect medication. The answer is not unsupervised passage. Coordinate a safe alternative with the property manager or emergency services, so that the item is retrieved under supervision or by an authorised person. In training, draw a mock access map that shows the clean route, the restricted zones, the signage and the escalation path to the property manager or an emergency service. Do not allow access through a restricted or unassessed zone.

instruction.heading: 6. PPE and respiratory protection decisions
instruction.body: PPE and respiratory protection depend on the access, the permitted tasks and the hazard characterisation. Identify the contaminant uncertainty, the worker's medical fitness and training needs, the fit-testing requirements and the local respiratory program. PPE is not a substitute for safe access, hazard characterisation or source control. A worker who offers a disposable dust mask for an unknown ash exposure is proposing an inadequate control. Never infer that a respirator is suitable from its appearance. Where the hazard is beyond the program, flag the case for a competent hygiene adviser. In training, compare PPE requests against a simulated hazard register and flag each case that needs a competent adviser.

instruction.heading: 7. Content salvage and material suitability
instruction.body: Catalogue the items, establish who owns them, set salvage priorities, and seek qualified guidance for heat-damaged electronics, fragile finishes and heritage objects. Secure the client's consent and record any repairability that is uncertain. A homeowner who asks that smoke-affected photographs and electronics be wiped immediately is asking for work that has not been assessed. Do not operate exposed electrical devices without authorisation. Keep a salvage register that distinguishes protected items, items needing restricted handling and items that need professional referral. In training, complete a mock salvage register using fictional items.

instruction.heading: 8. Controlled cleaning methods and limitations
instruction.body: Before selecting any cleaning method, assess the stability of the substrate, the contamination and any manufacturer restrictions. High-value or fragile finishes need controlled testing by an authorised specialist. Document any damage that was there before the work. A technician who proposes abrasive scrubbing of painted historic timber to remove staining is proposing a destructive method, and it must not proceed without approval and evidence that it is suitable. In training, evaluate three fictional materials and record a compatibility-test or referral decision for each one.

instruction.heading: 9. Chemical and odour-treatment boundaries
instruction.body: Treat each proposed chemical or air-treatment method as its own exposure decision. Review the safety data, the label permissions, the ventilation, the exclusion of occupants and the evidence that the method works. Some odour treatments create additional hazardous by-products, so a method that removes one odour may create another hazard. A vendor who recommends ozone treatment and solvent fogging while residents remain inside has proposed something that must be refused. No chemical mixing, fogging or ozone use in occupied spaces is permitted without verification and authority. In training, audit mock chemical treatment proposals for missing permissions, missing exposure controls and missing manufacturer instructions. No product, dilution or method is given in this lesson.

instruction.heading: 10. Waste segregation and environmental controls
instruction.body: Characterise waste before anyone moves it. Suspected asbestos, chemical containers, batteries and other hazardous residues may need specialist segregation and licensed handling. Record who will transport and who will receive each waste stream. Never classify unknown contaminated waste as general rubbish by default. A customer who asks cleaners to place charred debris and unknown insulation in normal bins is asking for something that must be refused. In training, complete a simulated waste-transfer log and identify the streams that need confirmation from the local authority or a specialist.

instruction.heading: 11. Records, damage mapping and insurer handoff
instruction.body: Build an impartial inventory with dated photographs, condition descriptions, locations, the client's decisions and any authorised disposal notes. Distinguish observed conditions from conclusions about cause or contamination clearance. An insurer may ask for before-and-after photographs while the owner disputes the removal of some items. Record both positions and the chain of custody. Do not present photographs as proof of structural or environmental safety. In training, produce a fictional photo log and claims handover that records the unknowns and the chain-of-custody limits.

instruction.heading: 12. Verification and safe handover boundaries
instruction.body: Verification checks the scope that was actually completed, the defects still unresolved, the independent testing needed, any moisture or odour concerns and the professional clearance that is still required. Report only the cleaning work that was done and the limitations that remain. When all visible soot has gone and a customer asks for a certificate stating that the home is safe, the answer is no. Cleaning completion is not a safe-to-occupy certificate and is not a contamination-free certificate. In training, draft a fact-based completion statement and a referral list for the qualified clearance or re-occupancy decisions.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
instruction.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: the release from the controlling authority is missing or unclear; the structure or utilities are unresolved; ash or residue is disturbed or uncharacterised; asbestos or legacy hazardous material may be present; there is unrestricted access to a restricted zone; the PPE or respirator is not suitable or verified; a destructive method or unknown chemical treatment is proposed; exposed electrical devices would be operated without authority; waste would be classified as general rubbish without characterisation; or a party asks for a safe-to-occupy or clearance statement. A stop-work decision is correct, so record it and restart only once the competent party confirms the scope in writing.

procedure: Stop work. Remain outside any restricted zone, and do not enter a building that has not been released by the controlling authority.
Confirm in writing the authority that controls access, the release it has given and the boundaries of that release.
Refer structural and utility hazards to qualified personnel. Do not operate damaged electrical equipment or do DIY repairs.
Treat ash and residue as uncertain. Keep the material undisturbed and refer it for qualified assessment.
If asbestos or legacy hazardous material may be present, stop, do not disturb the material, and refer to a competent assessor.
Set the exclusion zones and access routes with the site controller, and arrange a supervised alternative for any occupant who needs access.
Confirm the PPE, the respiratory program, the medical fitness and the fit before any worker enters an affected area.
Record the observations, the decisions, the referrals and the outstanding hazards. Issue a limited handover that reports only completed work and unresolved limitations.

workedExamples.situation: An owner asks for immediate salvage while the fire investigation has not released the premises.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must happen before any work starts?
workedExamples.reasoning: Ask who controls access and what has been formally released. Customer urgency is not verification. Remain outside, record the request, and request the written release from the responsible authority.

workedExamples.situation: A room looks stable, but photographs show a damaged electrical distribution board and a ceiling sag.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Damaged utilities and a sagging ceiling are stop-work hazards. No entry is made until qualified utility and structural personnel have resolved them, and no DIY repair is attempted.

workedExamples.situation: An installer proposes sweeping black powder from a burned office with a domestic vacuum.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Composition is uncertain and the residue must not be dry-disturbed. Refer for qualified assessment and an approved method for the site.

workedExamples.situation: A burned 1970s building has damaged ceiling sheeting and insulation of unknown composition.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not disturb the material. Issue a stop-work notification for suspected asbestos and identify the competent assessment still required. Removal, if needed, is licensed where the local rules require it.

workedExamples.situation: A vendor recommends ozone treatment and solvent fogging while residents remain inside.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How should the proposal be treated?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse. Each treatment is a separate exposure decision, and neither can proceed in occupied spaces without verification, permissions and exposure controls.

workedExamples.situation: The customer asks cleaners to put charred debris and unknown insulation into normal bins.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must be done with the waste?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse the general-bin route. Characterise the waste, identify the streams that need specialist or licensed handling, and record the transport and receiving parties.

workedExamples.situation: All visible soot has gone, and the customer asks for a certificate that the home is safe.
workedExamples.reasoning: Nothing beyond the completed cleaning. Cleaning completion does not establish that the home is safe to occupy or free of contamination. Issue a limited statement and a referral list for qualified clearance decisions.

commonErrors.error: Starting salvage because the owner is anxious, without a written release from the controlling authority.
commonErrors.prevention: Verify the release in writing. Customer urgency does not substitute for it.

commonErrors.error: Entering a room that looks stable despite visible damage to electrical or structural elements.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat visible damage as a stop-work hazard and refer to qualified personnel.

commonErrors.error: Sweeping or vacuuming ash and residue to make the area look clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the residue undisturbed and use only methods approved for the site after assessment.

commonErrors.error: Disturbing ceiling sheeting or insulation of unknown composition in an older building.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, do not disturb the material, and refer for competent asbestos assessment.

commonErrors.error: Using a disposable dust mask for an unknown ash exposure.
commonErrors.prevention: Flag the case for a competent hygiene adviser. Do not infer respirator suitability from appearance.

commonErrors.error: Scrubbing fire-affected historic finishes without testing.
commonErrors.prevention: Run a compatibility test or refer to an authorised specialist before any destructive method.

commonErrors.error: Running an odour treatment or ozone fogging while residents are inside.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse unverified treatments in occupied spaces. Review safety data, permissions and exposure controls first.

commonErrors.error: Putting charred debris or unknown insulation into general bins.
commonErrors.prevention: Characterise the waste and route suspect streams to specialist segregation and licensed handling.

commonErrors.error: Giving a safe-to-occupy certificate after visible soot is removed.
commonErrors.prevention: Limit the handover to the completed cleaning and the unresolved limitations, and refer clearance to the qualified party.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This module does not grant authority to enter, release, re-occupy, disturb or certify a fire-damaged building, or to handle waste. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

Fire-scene release, structural and utility isolation, asbestos assessment and removal, and some waste handling are restricted to competent and, where the law requires, licensed people. In Victoria, non-friable asbestos can be removed under a Class B licence, but fire-damaged material that has become friable, or may become friable during the work, needs a Class A licence (WorkSafe Victoria pages reviewed 4 May 2023 and 8 November 2023).
Sources recorded for this lesson include WorkSafe Victoria, NSW and WA asbestos guidance, and US EPA and California guidance. US and California sources are not Australian law.

Fire-damaged asbestos-containing material may become friable, so it must be treated as friable where its condition is uncertain or access is restricted. Do not disturb fire-damaged building products of unknown composition.
PPE and respiratory-protection requirements, including medical fitness and fit testing, follow the employer's program and the local rules.
No chemical, odour treatment, dilution, quantity or cleaning formula is given. Ozone and solvent methods are not to be used in occupied spaces without verification.
Cleaning completion is not a safe-to-occupy or contamination-free certificate. Clearance and re-occupancy decisions belong to a competent, authorised party.

summary: Fire work starts with the written release from the controlling authority. Urgency is not verification.
Visible damage to structures and utilities is a stop-work hazard. Refer to qualified personnel.
Ash and residue are uncertain. Keep them undisturbed and assess them first.
Older buildings may contain asbestos. Do not disturb unknown material.
Set the exclusion zones and arrange supervised access. No unsupervised passage.
PPE is matched to the hazard and verified. A dust mask is not a fire-residue control.
Chemical and odour treatments are separate exposure decisions. Refuse them in occupied spaces.
Characterise waste. Never default to general bins.
Keep an impartial record, and hand over only what was completed.

officialReferences.title: Bushfire recovery: asbestos clean-up
officialReferences.covers: Victorian licence classes only (Class A for friable, Class B for non-friable asbestos). Check the licence rules for your state or territory. Publisher: WorkSafe Victoria.

officialReferences.title: Demolition of fire-damaged buildings containing non-friable asbestos-containing material
officialReferences.covers: Victorian guidance on competent assessment and licence classes. Check the requirements for your state or territory. Publisher: WorkSafe Victoria.

officialReferences.title: Managing asbestos in emergencies and disasters
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary fetch. Storms, floods, bushfires and building fires can move, break or weaken asbestos materials. The page advises leaving asbestos in place or keeping it contained until a professional can help. For storms and floods, identifying asbestos needs a licensed asbestos assessor or occupational hygienist. For fire-damaged sites the page treats asbestos as friable, says clean-up should start only after the property is declared safe, and says all fire-damaged asbestos removal works must be undertaken by Class A licensed asbestos removalists. Publisher: NSW Asbestos Coordination Committee. Victorian and other state rules are not covered by this entry.

officialReferences.title: Asbestos safety after an emergency or disaster
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary fetch. Fires, floods and storms can damage buildings containing asbestos. Avoid sweeping or vacuuming debris, do not use high-pressure sprays, and do not enter a property until authorities confirm it is safe. Wear a P2 mask and protective clothing. If asbestos is suspected, contact a competent person or licensed asbestos assessor before clean-up starts. If asbestos is confirmed, a licensed asbestos removalist carries out the clean-up. For urgent removal, the removalist must phone WorkSafe and submit a notification within 24 hours. Clearance is still needed before people re-enter. Publisher: WorkSafe WA.

knowledgeChecks.question: An owner asks for immediate salvage while the fire investigation has not released the premises. What must happen first?
options: Start salvage, because the owner has the keys and the owner is the one who pays for the work
Ask who controls access and obtain the written release from the responsible authority before any work.
Start with the rooms the owner says are safe, since the owner knows the building best of all

knowledgeChecks.question: A room looks stable, but photographs show a damaged electrical distribution board and a sagging ceiling. Is entry permitted?
options: Yes, if the room looks stable and the ceiling has no obvious sign of movement or damage
Yes, if the worker does a quick repair first to make the board safe to use for the job
No. Stop work until qualified utility and structural personnel have resolved the hazards.

knowledgeChecks.question: An installer proposes sweeping black powder from a burned office with a domestic vacuum. What is correct?
options: Refuse. Keep the residue undisturbed and refer for qualified assessment and an approved method.
Proceed, because the room looks clean afterwards and the residue has been removed by the vacuum
Proceed if the vacuum has a fine filter and the worker wears a mask during the work

knowledgeChecks.question: A 1970s fire-damaged building has damaged ceiling sheeting and insulation of unknown composition. What is correct?
options: Remove the sheeting quickly before it falls, since the ceiling is a risk to the crew and occupants
Do not disturb the material. Issue a stop-work notification and identify the competent assessment still required.
Remove only the insulation, which is probably safe to handle once it is wet and bagged on site today

knowledgeChecks.question: A neighbouring tenant wants to walk through a partly damaged corridor to collect medication. What is the response?
options: Let the tenant through quickly with a warning to watch their step, since the path is short and clear
Refuse all help and tell the tenant to wait, since nothing can be done for the medication until morning
Refuse unsupervised passage and arrange a supervised alternative with the property manager or emergency services.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker offers a disposable dust mask for an unknown ash exposure. What is correct?
options: Refuse as an inadequate control, and flag the case for a competent hygiene adviser.
Accept, because a mask is better than nothing and the worker has nothing else available
Accept if the worker has used it before on similar ash jobs at other sites

knowledgeChecks.question: A homeowner asks for smoke-affected photographs and electronics to be wiped immediately. What is correct?
options: Wipe them now, because the owner asked and the owner is the one who pays for the whole clean-up of the house
Hold them, record the request and refer the items for assessment and owner consent. Do not operate exposed electrical devices.
Plug in the electronics to test them, then wipe them down once they are confirmed to be working properly for the owner

knowledgeChecks.question: A technician proposes abrasive scrubbing of painted historic timber to remove staining. What is correct?
options: Scrub it, because it is the fastest way to remove the staining from the historic timber today
Scrub a small hidden area, then decide whether the rest of the timber can be treated
Do not proceed without approval and evidence that the method is suitable. Test or refer first.

knowledgeChecks.question: A vendor recommends ozone treatment and solvent fogging while residents remain inside. What is correct?
options: Refuse. Each treatment is an exposure decision, and it cannot proceed in occupied spaces without verification and permissions.
Proceed, because odour treatment is needed urgently and the residents have asked for the work to be done now
Proceed if the residents leave the house for an hour or two, so the treatment can be done safely and quickly

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer asks cleaners to place charred debris and unknown insulation in normal bins. What is correct?
options: Agree, because the bins are collected every week and the waste will be removed with the household rubbish
Refuse. Characterise the waste and route suspect streams to specialist segregation and licensed handling.
Agree if the customer signs for it, since the customer takes responsibility for the waste after it leaves

knowledgeChecks.question: An insurer wants before-and-after photographs while the owner disputes the removal of some items. What is correct?
options: Give the insurer the photographs and call the dispute resolved, since the insurer has the final say on it
Withhold the photographs from everyone until the dispute ends, since the photos could be used in the case
Record both positions with dated photographs and chain of custody, and separate observations from conclusions.

knowledgeChecks.question: All visible soot has been removed, and the customer asks for a certificate that the home is safe. What is correct?
options: Refuse the safe-to-occupy certificate. Report only the completed cleaning and refer clearance to the qualified party.
Issue the certificate, because the soot is gone and the kitchen and the rest of the home look clean
Issue a certificate for the kitchen only, since the kitchen is the room the customer uses most often
